items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique affectant Palo Alto.

ReliaQuest confirmed that the Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting a Palo Alto vulnerability patched in May

Ransomware groups continue to target a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks products, despite a security patch being released five months ago, according to ReliaQuest.

The cyber threat detection provider warned in a social media advisories posted on October 9 that multiple groups, including the Qilin and Settra ransomware operations, are actively targeting CVE-2026-0257 to establish unauthorized VPN sessions and gain initial access to internal networks.

CVE-2026-0257 is an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access that affects several Palo Alto Networks products, including PAN-OS versions 10.2.0, 11.1.0, 11.2.0 and 12.1.0 and two versions of Prisma Access (10.2.0 and 11.2.0).

It was discovered by Palo Alto Networks, which disclosed it on May 13, 2026, allocating it a 7.8 severity score (CVSS) and a “highest” urgency rating.

Alternatively, the vulnerability enrichment team at the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD), part of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), allocated the flaw a critical severity rating of 9.1.

Palo Alto also released fixed versions that customers were urged to deploy to mitigate the threat, saying it had “become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.”

Matthieu Rouvre Directeur Commercial Europe du Sud, Cribl, © GS Mag GSM : comment présenteriez-vous votre parcours ? M. R. : je suis dans l'informatique depuis 2010 : EMC, puis le logiciel chez un éditeur racheté par Cisco, et plus de six ans dans l'univers de la donnée et de l'observabilité avant de rejoindre Cribl en juin 2024. Je couvre la France, l'Espagne, l'Italie et le Portugal. GSM : à quel problème répond Cribl ? M. R. : les volumes de données progressent d'environ 27 % par an selon IDC, quand les budgets augmentent de 7 % au mieux. Placés entre les sources, comme les pare-feu, et les destinations, comme le SIEM (gestion des informations et des événements de sécurité), nous collectons et routons la donnée de façon agnostique, avec un filtrage qui réduit de 30 à 70 % le volume transmis. Créée en 2017, l'entreprise annonce aujourd'hui plus de 350 millions de dollars de revenu récurrent annuel. GSM : un exemple concret ? M. R. : dans le cadre d'une migration d'un systeme de sécurité, plutôt que de tout envoyer vers le palier de stockage le plus coûteux, nous y avons seulement copier 15 à 20 % des données, le reste reste sur des stockages moins chers

Daiichi Kosho says a supply chain breach has exposed personal data on over eight million karaoke customers

One of Japan’s biggest karaoke box operators has revealed a data breach at a supplier which it claims may have exposed personal information of over eight million customers.

Daiichi Kosho has several popular brands including Big Echo, one of the country’s largest karaoke box chains, and also manufactures karaoke entertainment systems.

It published a statement on October 8 claiming an incident at Nippon Columbia Group (NCG), a Japanese entertainment group which handles customer information for the firm.

“According to NCG, between October 1 and October 2, 2026, a malware infection was discovered on one of their employees' devices (a PC), and the device was isolated from the network on October 2. Following an investigation into the scope of the impact by NCG, we received a report from NCG on October 5,” it explained.

“Personal data related to work outsourced to us was temporarily stored on the device in question, and we cannot rule out the possibility that this data may have been leaked.”

Signal de veille — Help Net Security.

Let’s Encrypt moves to a 64-day default certificate lifetime on February 10, 2027, and admins with hardcoded renewals need to update them.

Subscribers who already use Let’s Encrypt’s optional 45-day or 6-day certificates are not affected.

The organization expects the last 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027, and will not revoke any valid certificates during the transition.

The move to shorter certificate lifetimes “reduces the risk of key compromise and mis-issuance,” said Sarah Gran of the Internet Security Research Group (ISRG), the nonprofit that runs Let’s Encrypt.

“As a nonprofit we see it as part of our mission to make this change to advance security for everyone using the Web globally,” Gran added.

The 64-day period prepares users for default lifetimes of 45 days in 2028.

Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, and recommends testing there before the production switch.

Signal de veille — The Register.

If you thought everyone was into chatbots, think again: about half of US adults never use the AI tools, and most have no interest in starting. According to Pew Research Center, older adults are the least likely to use chatbots, with roughly three-quarters of those aged 65 and older saying they never use them. That may be expected, yet more than half (58 percent) of adults aged 50 to 64 don't use them either. Those aged 18 to 29 use chatbots the most, at 66 percent, however even a third of them say they never do. About four in ten under 50 report not using them at all. Across all adults, 51 percent are chatbot refuseniks, so users are - just barely - the minority. Pew asked non-users to choose from five possible reasons. Six in ten cited simple lack of interest as a major factor, followed by the more familiar concerns of data privacy and the accuracy of chatbot answers. Some Reg readers might suspect older people avoid chatbots because they lack tech-savviness, but fewer than a third cited not knowing how to use them as a major reason. The authors of the survey also found fewer than one in five worried about what others might think of them for using the technology, so social stigma isn’t the deterrent either.
